strengths: Addresses genuine gaps in existing benchmarks by providing the first unified framework combining three modalities, four languages, and both short/long-form contexts with human annotations
High-quality professional annotations: trained linguists for transcription, professional translators for multilingual content, and expert NLP annotators for QA pairs
Comprehensive evaluation of 21 publicly available models across multiple categories (LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, MLLMs), providing valuable empirical insights
Well-motivated data source using recent ACL 2023 presentations, mitigating data contamination concerns while providing naturally multimodal content
Thoughtful benchmark design with structured QA creation (modality labels, question type distribution) and dual prompt variants (MCIFfix/MCIFmix) to test robustness
Open license (CC-BY 4.0) and commitment to release code upon acceptance support research reproducibility
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and comprehensive appendices documenting the data creation process
weaknesses: Critical issue: Sections 5.2 (Effect of Modalities Integration) and 5.3 (Breakdown on Question Answering) are incomplete with only 'Work in progress...' placeholders, representing a major gap in results and analysis for a top-tier submission
No inter-annotator agreement (IAA) statistics reported for QA pairs despite this being standard and essential for benchmark validation; only 16 annotators, all students/authors, raises bias concerns
Small dataset scale (21 talks in core benchmark, 100 total) is modest compared to comprehensive benchmarks; raises questions about generalizability and statistical power
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance analysis on any results; negative BERTScores (e.g., -11.3) suggest baseline rescaling issues not adequately addressed
Limited multilingual scope: only 4 languages selected partly due to budget constraints; all source content is English, so 'crosslingual' aspect is limited to instruction-translation
Narrow domain focus: all content from scientific NLP talks; generalization to other scientific domains or non-scientific contexts unclear and underdiscussed
Missing ablations on key design choices (segment length, metric selection) and no error analysis or failure case studies to understand model behavior
Evaluation methodology concerns: BERTScore (dated metric) lacks theoretical justification for baseline rescaling; QA distribution enforced artificially rather than reflecting realistic patterns

strengths: Addresses an important gap by combining multimodal, crosslingual, and instruction-following evaluation in a unified benchmark
Professional data annotation with linguists for transcription, expert annotators for QA creation, and professional translators with scientific expertise
Comprehensive coverage across 3 modalities, 4 languages, 13 tasks, and both short/long-form contexts (~10 hours of video)
Extensive baseline evaluation with 21 state-of-the-art models across multiple model categories (LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, MLLMs)
Includes two prompt variants (MCIFfix and MCIFmix) to evaluate robustness to instruction reformulation
Permissive CC-BY 4.0 license encourages broad adoption and reproducibility
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Results section explicitly incomplete with prominent warning; entire subsections marked 'Work in progress' (Sections 5.2 and 5.3), suggesting premature submission
Dataset is very small (21 talks for main eval, 100 total samples, ~220 QA pairs) compared to comparable benchmarks, raising statistical significance concerns
Data contamination risk inadequately addressed—ACL 2023 content available for 1+ year with no evidence it is absent from recent model training data
Severely limited domain specificity—all data from scientific talks only (NLP/ACL domain), limiting generalizability of findings to other domains and content styles
Limited language diversity—4 languages selected by convenience (budget and author availability) rather than linguistic representativeness; missing entire language families
Insufficient evaluation methodology: no inter-annotator agreement metrics reported, no human evaluation, no statistical significance testing, non-standard BERTScore rescaling, single data split
Shallow analysis of results—mostly descriptive tables without error categorization, qualitative failure analysis, language-specific patterns, or investigation of task difficulty
QA pair creation by expert annotators (students and authors in NLP/ML) without external validation; potential bias and no inter-annotator agreement reported
Restricted to models <20B parameters due to computational constraints, excluding important recent models and limiting scope of conclusions
Reproducibility gaps: code released 'upon acceptance,' internal ASR/MT systems confidential, generation settings brief

strengths: Addresses clear and important gap: first human-annotated multimodal, crosslingual, instruction-following benchmark with both short and long-form contexts
High-quality dataset construction with professional linguists and translators, structured QA design with enforced distributions, and principled modality labeling (A/V/AV/NA)
Comprehensive evaluation of 21 models (LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, MLLMs) across 13 tasks in 4 languages with two prompt variants (MCIFfix/MCIFmix) testing robustness
Valuable empirical findings: long-form recognition as bottleneck, MLLMs more robust than specialized models on long contexts, significant degradation under prompt variation
Strong reproducibility practices with detailed appendices, model configurations, and commitment to open release under CC-BY 4.0 license
weaknesses: Critical Issue: Sections 5.2 and 5.3 marked 'Work in progress...' with placeholder text—substantial promised analyses are missing and manuscript appears incomplete at submission
Relatively modest scale for a benchmark paper: 21 core talks (2 hours), 220 QA pairs total, and 100 samples for summarization are small compared to recent benchmarks like MMMU (11.5K questions)
Missing critical analyses: no inter-annotator agreement (IAA) reported for QA pairs, no quality assurance metrics, minimal failure mode analysis, no cross-lingual transfer or task-level breakdowns

Methodological concerns: QA created by authors/students with potential native-speaker bias, summarization uses paper abstracts rather than independent human summaries, language selection driven partly by budget constraints
Domain-specific scope limited to scientific/NLP talks (ACL 2023) raises generalization concerns for 'general-purpose' MLLM evaluation claims
Evaluation methodology gaps: BERTScore used without human validation, no inter-rater reliability reported, incomplete task coverage across languages (e.g., ASR English-only)

strengths: Addresses clear gap in existing benchmarks by systematically evaluating crosslingual and multimodal instruction-following
Thoughtful parallel design across all dimensions (3 modalities × 4 languages × 2 context types) enabling controlled comparisons
High-quality human annotations with professional transcriptions, expert QA pairs, and detailed guidelines
Comprehensive evaluation of 23 models with multiple metrics and thorough ablation studies
Provides useful and actionable insights about model limitations (long-form, multimodal integration, summarization, fine-grained understanding)
Strong reproducibility efforts with released code, guidelines, and all resources under CC-BY 4.0
Well-presented paper with clear organization and informative visualizations
weaknesses: Small dataset size (100 samples, ~10 hours) limits statistical power and representativeness; no confidence intervals or significance tests
Single domain restriction (ACL scientific presentations) severely limits generalizability and raises questions about transfer to other domains
Limited linguistic diversity with only 4 well-resourced languages; claim of 'typological diversity' is overstated and no low-resource languages included
Evaluation metric concerns: BERTScore known to have limitations for semantic tasks; single-reference COMET may miss valid variations; no human evaluation validation
Lacks statistical rigor with single train/test split, no cross-validation, and no inter-annotator agreement reported for QA creation
Shallow crosslingual analysis with results mostly aggregated across languages and per-language patterns undiscussed
Findings are largely confirmatory (long-form is harder, multimodal integration fails, summarization difficult) rather than surprising or novel
Limited analysis of why multimodal integration fails and no investigation of potential solutions
Context length exploration incomplete with large gap between short-form (~16s) and long-form (~10h) but no intermediate lengths tested
Missing comparisons with related benchmarks (VideoMME, MF²) and no validation against human performance baselines

strengths: Addresses genuine gaps in existing benchmarks by providing the first unified evaluation of multimodal (text/speech/video), crosslingual (4 languages), and long-form instruction-following capabilities
Thoughtful parallel design fully aligned across modalities, languages, and context types enables systematic ablation studies
High-quality dataset curation with professional linguists, detailed annotation guidelines, and human verification of translations
Comprehensive baseline evaluation covering 23 diverse models across multiple modalities (LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, MLLMs)
Strong reproducibility support including detailed prompts, generation settings, MCIFfix/MCIFmix variants, and promised code/output release
Detailed analysis with useful breakdowns by modality, context length, question type, and language
weaknesses: Dataset scale severely insufficient: only 21 talks (~2 hours, ~16k words) for primary analyses; 100 total for summarization. Modern benchmarks have hundreds to thousands of examples. This limits statistical power and generalizability
Single domain (NLP/academic talks) with no evidence of generalizability to other sectors or application contexts

Limited scientific novelty: primarily organizational contribution with no new evaluation metrics, architectural insights, or analysis methods. Findings are unsurprising (long-form is hard, summarization is difficult)

Problematic evaluation methodology: BERTScore for QA measures surface similarity not correctness; using paper abstracts as summaries is crude and unvalidated; no human evaluation or inter-annotator agreement scores provided
Significant data contamination risk: ACL 2023 papers/videos are publicly available; many models may have seen this data during training. Limited mitigation strategies implemented

Unfair model comparisons: mixing 20B parameter LLMs with 2.8B MLLMs, open-weight vs. proprietary models, and models with different training objectives and data. No ablation studies isolating architectural contributions
Insufficient error analysis: no systematic failure mode categorization, no investigation of whether failures stem from inherent incapability vs. fine-tuning gaps, limited manual inspection
Narrow language scope: only 4 languages (German, Italian are low-resource choices); primarily tests English→{DE,IT,ZH} translation rather than true multilingual capabilities

Abstractsas gold summaries inadequately validated: paper abstracts are meta-summaries for researchers, not actual talk content summaries. No human validation of abstract quality or correlation with talk content
Limited robustness analysis: only 2 prompt variants provided insufficient to establish generalization; default generation parameters used without task-specific optimization

strengths: First truly parallel multimodal-crosslingual instruction-following benchmark with full alignment across 3 modalities, 4 languages, and all task dimensions
High-quality human annotation with professional transcription, translation, and expert QA creation supported by detailed guidelines and verification procedures

Comprehensive empirical evaluation of 23 models across 4 categories with systematic ablations and detailed failure analysis revealing important insights (summarization difficulty, poor speech-video integration, long-form degradation)
Well-motivated design addressing clear gaps in existing benchmarks (English-only, single modality, short-form only, synthetic data)
Excellent reproducibility and open science practices: CC-BY 4.0 license, complete documentation of models/prompts/settings, code release commitment, and transparent ethical considerations
Thoughtful benchmark variants (MCIFfix/MCIFmix) for assessing both consistency and robustness to prompt variation
Clear presentation with well-organized structure, comprehensive figures/tables, and detailed appendices
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale (100 samples total) raises questions about statistical power and generalization, though quality-over-quantity is appropriate for benchmarks

Restricted language and domain scope: 4 languages (3 Indo-European + Chinese), all well-resourced, limiting test of true multilingual capabilities; single domain (NLP scientific talks) limits generalizability
Evaluation relies exclusively on automatic metrics (WER, COMET, BERTScore) without human evaluation despite creating high-quality references, particularly problematic for QA/summarization
Missing inter-annotator agreement statistics and kappa values; no systematic annotation quality analysis beyond guideline documentation
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or systematic analysis of result variance across languages and model pairs
Limited linguistic analysis: results per-language but minimal investigation of how linguistic phenomena affect performance or language-pair-specific challenges
Model coverage limited to <20B parameters due to computational constraints, excluding frontier models that may have different characteristics
No systematic data contamination detection despite using recent materials; no baseline models (random, majority) for contextualizing absolute performance levels
Prompt variability testing limited to 10 alternatives per macro-task with relatively formulaic variations; no adversarial prompt testing
